chapter: Rhythm Club, studio dates and the 1930s big bands
title: Getting copies of one's records
summary: Musicians bought copies or got one from the leader; records were a side thing next to live performance.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: Concerning a couple of other things, uh --

Oh, when musicians were -- say, you were in an orchestra or you were among a select group of musicians who play with Teddy Wilson or you recorded with Putney (Inaudible) Dandridge or Red Allen, were you able to get copies of the records that you were on from the company; or, did you have to go out to buy them?
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943

Or -- I mean, you did say before that a lot of times a record wouldn't be released till maybe several months or until even a year later. But could you go buy the records at the record company, and say, "Hey, I understand the record is out and I'm on that record. I'd like to hear it." Give it to my family or --

Oh, we would go and buy it. If the band leader had some, he would give us one, or something like that. But to tell you the truth, I don't think those musicians -- The time we come up, we wasn't too much record-conscious, you know. This was something like a side thing, you know. It was something like -- Like I say, like before (inaudible) --
The live performance was more important.
Yeah. It was just like a side thing, you know.
